signals.headline: Ottawa Promises 500 MW of Sovereign AI Compute as Large AI Firms Crowd Out Canadian Startups
signals.theFact: The federal government is promising 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute, using backstops and offtake agreements to encourage private investment, but Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada has not set a timeline, pricing or access rules for that capacity. Sean Mullin of the Munk School, who helped launch the strategy, says firms such as Meta, Google and OpenAI are “desperate for compute” and can lock up data-centre output for five to ten years, leaving Canadian startups to buy capacity outside the country.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: Ocean Falls builds local, on-prem inference in B.C. so organizations that need data to stay under Canadian law don’t have to wait for a share of a 500 MW national pledge that still has no timeline or access rules.

signals.headline: Dell and Microsoft move Nvidia B300 inference on-prem as sovereignty drives buyers
signals.theFact: Dell and Microsoft are expanding their Azure Local partnership to run enterprise AI inference on Nvidia HGX B300 systems in customer-controlled environments, after Microsoft said at Ignite on Nov. 17 that Foundry Local is generally available on Azure Local. In IDC's June 2026 survey, 85 per cent of enterprises said their AI workloads need both on-premises and public cloud, and sovereignty and latency each influenced 51 per cent of respondents, ahead of cost at 42 per cent.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: The big vendors are now packaging on-prem sovereign inference for regulated buyers, and an Ocean Falls MicroNode puts that capability inside B.C. so the data never leaves the customer's custody.

signals.headline: Alberta proposes 600-metre setbacks for big data centres, with brownfield sites exempt
signals.theFact: Alberta's Bill 42 would bar data centres that draw 10 MW or more from being built within 600 metres of the nearest home or on the province's highest-quality farmland, and the province said about 30 per cent of current proposals would likely be affected. Technology Minister Nate Glubish said existing brownfield sites and designated industrial zones could be exempt from the setbacks, and the bill would also make data centres pay for their own power infrastructure and use close to zero water for cooling.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: Alberta is writing brownfield exemptions and sub-10 MW thresholds into law, and those are the two things Ocean Falls already builds its site selection around.

signals.headline: Hyperscale campuses are worth up to $45B, but insurers top out at $5–10B
signals.theFact: A new LGT Capital Partners paper says AI hyperscale campuses carry $30 billion to $45 billion or more in insurable value, while the conventional property market's effective limit for a single risk generally tops out at $5 billion to $10 billion. LGT cites market estimates that one-third to half of data-centre value is currently uninsured, and Moody's analysts noted in March 2026 that investors including Blackstone reportedly passed on data-centre debt because coverage was insufficient.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: A sub-10 MW site keeps each insured value small enough for ordinary property capacity, and it is the kind of risk a captive program can write, while hyperscale campuses go partly uninsured.

signals.headline: Vancouver council votes unanimously for third-party impact checks on AI data centres
signals.theFact: Vancouver city council unanimously passed Coun. Lucy Maloney's motion directing staff to urgently develop a Bulk Data Storage Public Impact Requirement. Before any rezoning or permitting, applicants would have to commission a third-party assessment of water, greenhouse gas emissions, air contaminants, noise and heat, mitigation including heat recovery, and employment impacts.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: As Vancouver adds third-party impact studies for big urban data centres, small brownfield sites and on-prem MicroNodes with a light local footprint become the easier way to get compute built in B.C.

signals.headline: B.C. has 800 MW of data-centre asks, a 400 MW target, and no decision yet
signals.theFact: BC Hydro's 2026 Call for Demand drew 15 applications totalling close to 800 megawatts, about twice the province's two-year allocation target of up to 400 MW, and the September 2026 notification date has slipped until after the provincial government transition. The delay lands as Telus pulls out of two Vancouver AI data centres and says it will focus on expanding its existing Kamloops site.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: Sites that ask for less than 10 MW stay out of B.C.'s competitive call and use the ordinary connection process, so Ocean Falls' sub-10 MW brownfield sites skip the queue that has stalled 800 MW of requests.

signals.headline: Ontario Is Writing Data Centre Grid Rules Into Its Market Rules, for Every Load Above 10 MW
signals.theFact: Ontario’s IESO is moving its technical requirements for large computational loads into the province’s Market Rules, with the proposed amendments going to a webinar on November 19 and the rule change targeted for Q2 2027. The requirements cover connection, reactive power, oscillation, ramp rates and ride-through, and apply to every transmission-connected computational load and to distribution-connected loads above 10 MW.
signals.oceanFallsAngle: Ocean Falls’ sub-10 MW brownfield siting stays under the size where grid operators from B.C. to Ontario are adding competitive calls and new technical obligations for data centres.
